zh.summary: 用有明確目標、但不透露操作答案的任務觀察使用者，將觀察、推論與改版假設分開。
objectives: 設計缺漏、補正與匯出的目標任務。
記錄操作與提示介入，不把推論當觀察。
用小範圍改善與再試用檢驗設計假設。

readingGuide.goal: 設計缺漏、補正與匯出的目標任務。
readingGuide.startingPoint: 可操作的本機第三切片、一位自願同儕、合成任務卡與空白紀錄表。
readingGuide.route: 先理解情境與原理，再對照工作坊檔案，最後留下可核對的操作與審查紀錄。
readingGuide.output: 一份匿名任務觀察紀錄與可再測的設計假設；尚未有人試用時保留未執行。

sections.heading: 這一課要學的核心
paragraphs:
這一課要學的核心是：

軟體功能正常，不代表使用者真的會用。要知道系統是否好用，就讓使用者親自完成真實任務，觀察他在哪裡順利、在哪裡卡住，再根據證據改善設計。

sections.heading: 一、什麼是任務導向易用性測試？
paragraphs:
先想像你開了一家餐廳，設計了一台自助點餐機。

工程師測試後告訴你：

- 觸控螢幕正常。

- 菜單可以顯示。

- 加入購物車功能正常。

- 信用卡付款正常。

- 訂單確實送進廚房。

工程師認為系統通過測試。

但實際開放客人使用時，卻發生了這些問題：

客人找不到素食餐點、不知道怎麼取消已選品項、付款後不確定有沒有成功，甚至有人因為害怕重複扣款而不敢繼續操作。

這時候你會發現：

工程師證明了系統「可以運作」，卻沒有證明客人「能夠順利完成點餐」。

這就是為什麼需要 Task-based Usability Test。

它不是請使用者隨便看看畫面，也不是只問他「你覺得好不好用？」。

而是給他一個具體目標，例如：

> 你今天要幫三位朋友點餐，其中一位不吃肉。請完成點餐並確認訂單成功送出。

然後觀察他能否自行找到菜單、處理飲食限制、修改數量、付款並確認結果。

這個方法最重要的精神是：

告訴使用者要完成什麼，不要告訴他應該按哪個按鈕。

教材也特別強調，測試中要把實際觀察、可能的原因與後續改善假設分開。

sections.heading: 二、這種測試和一般軟體測試有什麼不同？
paragraphs: 可以把軟體品質分成四個不同的問題來檢查。

blocks.caption: 表 1｜二、這種測試和一般軟體測試有什麼不同？
rows: 介面自動化測試 UI Test
按鈕和畫面運作正常嗎？
點擊結帳是否進入付款頁
使用者能自行完成工作嗎？
客人是否找得到取消訂單功能
系統能否阻止不當操作？
A 使用者能否偷看 B 的訂單

paragraphs:
這些測試互相補充，不能彼此取代。

尤其要理解：系統可以同時通過所有自動化測試，卻在易用性測試中失敗。
### 易用性的三個重要面向

blocks.caption: 表 2｜二、這種測試和一般軟體測試有什麼不同？

paragraphs:
例如兩個人都成功完成網路掛號，但甲只花兩分鐘，乙花十五分鐘，而且一直擔心是否預約成功。

兩人都完成任務，卻不代表體驗品質相同。

sections.heading: 三、實際要怎麼進行？完整流程
paragraphs: 用以下六步，將研究問題連到下一次驗證。

blocks.caption: 圖 1｜任務導向易用性測試的工作流程
blocks.description: 箭頭表示六個研究步驟的順序；再測後依結果決定下一個問題，並非已證明改善有效。

items.title: 決定要研究的問題
items.body: 例如：使用者能不能發現資料缺漏？

items.title: 設計有目標的任務
items.body: 只交代目的、情境和必要資料。

items.title: 讓使用者自行操作
items.body: 主持人不提供操作答案。

items.title: 記錄可觀察的證據
items.body: 行為、停頓、錯誤、協助、結果。

items.title: 提出原因假設並改善
items.body: 先選一個有證據支持的問題。

items.title: 使用相同目標重新驗證
items.body: 確認改善是否真的有效。

paragraphs: 這是一個持續改進的循環，而不是做完一次就結束。英國政府的易用性研究指引也強調，測試任務應該具體、可信、貼近使用者情境，但不能暗示完成方法。

sections.heading: 四、不同產業應該怎麼設計測試任務？
paragraphs: 關鍵是把「操作指令」轉換為「工作目標」。

blocks.caption: 表 3｜四、不同產業應該怎麼設計測試任務？
rows: 你想預約下週的內科門診，請完成預約
有一份資料需要交給主管審查，請準備報告
你不想買其中一件商品了，請修改訂單
請取得本學期的成績紀錄
打開追蹤功能，輸入編號
客戶詢問包裹到哪裡了，請找到最新狀態

paragraphs:
注意：適合的任務不一定比較短，重點是不要把介面設計應該提供的線索，提前由主持人說出來。

否則你測到的就不是介面有多清楚，而是參與者有多會遵從指令。

sections.heading: 五、最重要的研究能力：區分觀察、推論與假設
paragraphs:
這是本課值得特別學習的部分。

假設你正在測試一套銀行報告系統。

使用者修改了資料，但沒有重新產生報告，直接下載舊版檔案。

你可能立刻認為：

「這個人一定不知道資料修改後必須重新檢查。」

但你其實不知道他的想法。

我們應該把事情拆成三層：

blocks.caption: 表 4｜五、最重要的研究能力：區分觀察、推論與假設
rows: 使用者修改資料後，未重新執行檢核，直接下載報告
使用者可能以為修改資料會自動更新報告
如果修改後顯示「結果已過期，請重新檢核」，可能減少下載舊報告的情況

paragraphs:
三者的差別很大。

觀察是實際發生的事；推論是可能的解釋；假設則是準備透過新測試驗證的主張。

例如，使用者也可能知道必須重新檢核，只是當時分心，或者系統的舊報告仍顯示為最新版本。

因此，不能直接把「可能」寫成「事實」。

這種區分不只適用 UX，也適用科學研究、醫療診斷、資安事件調查與企業管理。

sections.heading: 六、如何記錄一次測試？
paragraphs: 下面是一份簡化的紀錄表。

blocks.caption: 圖 2｜易用性測試觀察表（虛構示例）
rows: 修改資料後取得最新報告
修改資料後，未重新檢核即下載
未取得符合要求的最新報告
不清楚報告需要重新產生
標記舊結果並引導重新檢核
讓其他符合目標族群的參與者完成同類任務

paragraphs: 這只是教學示例，不代表曾經進行真人測試。可能原因是推論，改善假設仍待再測。

這只是教學示例，不代表曾經進行真人測試。

有三種完成情況必須分清楚：獨立完成、協助完成、未完成。

如果主持人提醒參與者應按哪個按鈕，然後他才成功完成工作，不能記成獨立完成。

同樣地，如果要量測完成時間，應先約定何時開始與結束、協助時間如何計算，避免每個人的數據定義不同。

sections.heading: 七、觀察到問題之後，應該怎麼改善？
paragraphs:
延續前面的例子。

假設使用者不知道修改資料後需要重新產生報告。

設計團隊可以嘗試提供更清楚的系統狀態：

blocks.caption: 圖 3｜報告狀態：改版前與設計提案
blocks.description: 上下兩區比較兩種設計，沒有操作順序箭頭。示意介面，非實際系統；動作文字不能執行下載或檢核。

items.title: 改版前
items.body:
報告管理
資料已修改
下載報告

items.title: 改版後的設計提案
items.body:
報告需要重新檢核
資料已經變更，目前的報告不再代表最新資料。完成檢核後才能下載最新報告。
重新檢核並更新報告

paragraphs:
這裡運用了兩項重要 UX 設計原則：

Visibility of System Status（系統狀態可見性）：使用者應該清楚知道目前發生什麼事。

Error Prevention（預防錯誤）：比起讓人下載錯誤報告後再補救，最好先降低錯誤操作發生的機會。

這兩項都是 Nielsen Norman Group 整理的十大易用性啟發式原則。

不過，提出設計改善，不等於已經證明改善有效。

應該再讓參與者完成同類任務，確認他是否能辨認報告狀態，以及能否取得正確結果。若要比較改版前後的效果，也需要留意參與者熟悉程度與測試條件的差異。

sections.heading: 八、常見的四種誤區
paragraphs: 以下四種判斷會影響參與者選擇、主持方式及結果解讀。
### 誤區一：找朋友試用一次，沒問題就代表產品好用。
朋友能幫你發現初步問題，但如果真正使用者是護理師、銀行授信人員或倉儲管理員，仍需要找具有相關工作經驗的人參與。少數人的結果不能直接推廣至全體使用者。
### 誤區二：測試時不可以給任何協助。
可以協助，但要記錄何時、為什麼、給了什麼提示，並區分獨立完成和協助完成。對真正卡住的人，適度協助有時能讓測試繼續蒐集其他問題的證據。
### 誤區三：使用者完成任務，就是沒有問題。
有人可能反覆嘗試十幾次才完成。雖然最後成功，但操作過程仍可能暴露設計缺陷。
### 誤區四：易用性測試可以取代安全和功能驗證。

不行。使用者覺得容易操作，不代表資料權限正確、計算結果準確，或系統符合無障礙要求。這些還需要獨立驗證。

另外，真人測試必須取得適當同意，說明紀錄用途。測試環境應優先使用安全的合成資料；若有錄影或真實個資，必須先處理保存、存取及隱私要求。

sections.heading: 九、把本課轉換成一項可以執行的工作
paragraphs:
你可以直接使用教材中的「收件資料檢核系統」進行一個小型實驗。

準備三個分階段任務：首先給使用者一筆文件類型缺漏的申請資料，請他判斷能不能產生完整報告；接著補充文件類型，請他取得可供同事核對的報告；最後撤回文件類型，請他判斷先前的檢核結果是否仍然有效。

建議讓一位自願同儕先試用，使用合成資料，不透露操作路徑，記錄實際行為、協助情況及完成結果。然後挑出一個最值得改善的問題，提出可以重新測試的設計假設。

這就完成了本課的最小實作。正式產品驗收則應擴大至具代表性的使用者、任務與環境。

sections.heading: 十、理解檢核
paragraphs:
情境題

某醫院開發了一套新的電子病歷系統。工程師已證明所有功能正常，但護士在試用時找不到「取消錯誤醫囑」的操作方式。

研究員認為：「護士一定是不熟悉電腦，所以才找不到。」

下列哪種處理方式最符合任務導向易用性測試的精神？

A. 先請護士參加電腦教育訓練，再結束測試

B. 告訴護士按哪個按鈕，只要成功就記錄通過

C. 記錄護士卡住的操作、詢問當時理解，再提出介面改善假設並重新測試

D. 因為程式測試通過，所以不用修改介面

本課最重要的結論： 易用性不是開發者自己認為操作簡單，而是目標使用者在特定情境下，能否有效、有效率且有合理信心地完成工作。要改善它，必須依靠真實行為的證據，而不只是直覺。

exercise.environment: 可操作的本機第三切片、一位自願同儕、合成任務卡與空白紀錄表。
steps: 說明目的與紀錄方式，取得同意後提供任務，不透露按鈕操作答案。
觀察缺漏、補正與變更，記錄協助、完成情況及實際行為。
分開觀察與推論，提出一項改善假設；修改後再安排一致目標的試用。
exercise.expected: 一份匿名任務觀察紀錄與可再測的設計假設；尚未有人試用時保留未執行。
exercise.check: 不編造參與者或結果，不把同儕單次觀察推成所有使用者結論。
exercise.cleanup: 停止測試服務，依已說明方式保存匿名紀錄，刪除不需要的合成下載。

en.summary: Observe users through goal-based tasks without giving away actions, separating observations, interpretations and redesign hypotheses.
objectives: Design goal-based tasks for omissions, correction and export.
Record actions and facilitator assistance without treating inference as observation.
Test design hypotheses through bounded changes and another trial.

readingGuide.goal: Design goal-based tasks for omissions, correction and export.
readingGuide.startingPoint: A working local third slice, one voluntary peer, synthetic task cards and a blank record.
readingGuide.route: Understand the situation and principles, compare the workshop files, then retain verifiable operation and review records.
readingGuide.output: An anonymous task-observation record and testable design hypothesis; mark unexecuted if no person has tried it.

sections.heading: The core idea
paragraphs: Working software does not establish that people can use it. Ask users to carry out realistic tasks, observe where they succeed or get stuck, and improve the design using that evidence.

sections.heading: 1. What is task-based usability testing?
paragraphs:
Imagine opening a restaurant with a self-service ordering kiosk. Engineers confirm that the touchscreen works, menus appear, items enter the cart, credit-card payments work, and orders reach the kitchen. The system passes their tests.

Customers then struggle to find vegetarian food, cancel selected items, or tell whether payment succeeded. Some stop because they fear being charged twice. The engineers established that the system operates; customers still need to complete an order successfully.

Task-based usability testing gives participants a specific goal instead of asking them to browse a screen or merely say whether they like it. For example: “Order for three friends, including one who does not eat meat, and confirm that the order was submitted successfully.” Observe whether they find the menu, handle the dietary restriction, change quantities, pay, and recognize the result.

Tell participants what they need to accomplish without naming the buttons to press. Keep observed behavior, possible explanations, and improvement hypotheses separate.

sections.heading: 2. How does it differ from other software tests?
paragraphs: Software quality raises four different questions.

blocks.caption: Table 1 | 2. How does it differ from other software tests?
rows: Does program logic produce the right result?
Do controls and screens operate as expected?
Does checkout open the payment page?
Can users complete the work themselves?
Can customers find how to cancel an order?
Does the system prevent unauthorized actions?
Can user A access user B’s order?

paragraphs: These tests complement one another. A system can pass all its automated tests and still fail a usability test.
### Three aspects of usability

blocks.caption: Table 2 | 2. How does it differ from other software tests?
rows: Whether the intended task is completed
How much effort does it require?

paragraphs: Two people may both book an outpatient appointment online, while one takes two minutes and the other takes fifteen and remains unsure whether the booking worked. Completion alone does not make the experiences equivalent.

sections.heading: 3. The complete workflow
paragraphs: Use the six stages below to connect a research question to a retest.

blocks.caption: Figure 1 | Task-based usability testing workflow
blocks.description: Arrows indicate the order of six research steps. Use retest findings to choose the next question; the sequence does not establish an improvement.

items.title: Choose a research question
items.body: For example: can users discover missing data?

items.title: Design a goal-based task
items.body: Provide only the purpose, context, and necessary data.

items.title: Let the participant act
items.body: The facilitator does not reveal the action path.

items.title: Record observable evidence
items.body: Actions, pauses, errors, assistance, and outcomes.

items.title: Hypothesize and improve
items.body: Choose one problem supported by evidence.

items.title: Retest with the same goal
items.body: Check whether the improvement actually works.

paragraphs: This is a continuing improvement cycle. After a retest, use the findings to decide the next research question. GOV.UK’s research guidance recommends specific, believable tasks that fit participants’ circumstances without suggesting the method of completion.

sections.heading: 4. Designing tasks across industries
paragraphs: Convert instructions about controls into goals about work.

blocks.caption: Table 3 | 4. Designing tasks across industries
rows: Book an internal medicine appointment for next week.
Prepare a report your supervisor can review.
Remove an item you no longer want from your order.
Obtain your grade record for this semester.
Open tracking and enter the number.
A customer asks where their parcel is; find its latest status.

paragraphs: A suitable task need not be shorter. The facilitator must leave the interface’s clues for participants to discover. Supplying those clues measures how well someone follows instructions instead of how clearly the design communicates.

sections.heading: 5. Distinguish observation, inference, and hypothesis
paragraphs: In a bank reporting system, a user changes data, does not regenerate the report, and downloads the old file. It is tempting to say, “They definitely do not know they must check again after editing.” Their thoughts have not yet been established. Separate the record into three layers.

blocks.caption: Table 4 | 5. Distinguish observation, inference, and hypothesis
rows: After changing data, the user downloaded a report without running validation again.
The user may expect data edits to update the report automatically.
Showing “Results are outdated; validate again” after edits may reduce old-report downloads.

paragraphs: An observation records what happened. An inference offers a possible explanation. A hypothesis proposes a claim to test. The user might already know that validation is needed but have been distracted, or the old report might still have appeared current. Keep possibilities distinct from facts. This discipline also applies to scientific research, medical diagnosis, security investigations, and business management.

sections.heading: 6. Recording a test
paragraphs: The following record illustrates how to preserve the scenario, behavior, result, possible cause, and proposed retest.

blocks.caption: Figure 2 | Usability observation record (fictional example)
rows: Obtain a current report after editing data
Downloaded after editing without validating again
Did not obtain the required current report
Mark old results and guide the user to validate again
Ask other participants from the target group to perform comparable tasks

paragraphs: A fictional teaching example, with no claim of human testing. The possible cause is an inference; the improvement hypothesis still needs a retest.

This is a fictional teaching example, with no claim that a human test occurred. Distinguish independent completion, assisted completion, and non-completion. If the facilitator identifies a button before the participant succeeds, record assisted completion. For timing, agree on start and end events and how assistance time will be handled before collecting measurements, so definitions stay consistent.

sections.heading: 7. Improving a design after observing a problem
paragraphs: Suppose the working explanation is that users do not realize edits require a newly generated report. The team can make the system’s status clearer. Compare the existing presentation with the proposed design below.

blocks.caption: Figure 3 | Report status: before and proposed redesign
blocks.description: The two stacked regions compare designs, without action-sequence arrows. Illustrative interface, not a live system; action labels do not download or validate anything.

items.title: Before
items.body:
Report management
Data has changed
Download report

items.title: Proposed redesign
items.body:
Report needs validation again
The data has changed. The current report no longer represents the latest data. Validate before downloading the latest report.
Validate again and update report

paragraphs:
Visibility of System Status means people can understand what is happening now. Error Prevention means reducing the opportunity to download the wrong report before having to repair the consequences. Both appear in Nielsen Norman Group’s ten usability heuristics.

A proposed improvement still needs evidence of its effect. Ask participants to perform comparable tasks again and check whether they recognize the report status and obtain the correct result. When comparing versions, consider differences in familiarity and testing conditions.

sections.heading: 8. Four common misunderstandings
paragraphs: These four judgments affect participant selection, facilitation, and interpretation.
### A friend’s successful attempt establishes usability

Friends can reveal early problems. When the actual audience is nurses, bank credit staff, or warehouse managers, recruit people with relevant work experience. A few participants’ results cannot automatically be generalized to everyone.
### Facilitators must never help

Help is possible. Record when, why, and what prompt was given, and distinguish assisted from independent completion. Helping someone who is completely stuck can allow the session to reveal other problems.
### Task completion means there is no problem
A person may need more than a dozen attempts before succeeding. Their process can still expose design problems even when the final result is correct.
### Usability testing replaces security and functional checks

Ease of use does not establish correct permissions, accurate calculations, or accessibility. Verify those separately. Obtain appropriate consent for human testing and explain how records will be used. Prefer safe synthetic data; establish retention, access, and privacy arrangements before recording video or handling real personal data.

sections.heading: 9. Turn the lesson into an executable task
paragraphs:
Use the course’s intake-data validation system for a small exercise. Prepare three tasks and provide their information in stages. First supply an application with a missing document type and ask whether a complete report can be produced. Then supply the document type and ask for a report a colleague can inspect. Finally withdraw the document type and ask whether the earlier validation result remains valid.

Invite one voluntary peer to try the synthetic tasks without revealing the action path. Record actual behavior, assistance, and completion. Choose one worthwhile problem and propose a design hypothesis that can be retested. This completes the lesson’s minimal practice; formal product acceptance requires representative users, tasks, and environments.

sections.heading: 10. Check your understanding
paragraphs:
A hospital develops an electronic medical record system. Engineers establish that its functions work, but nurses trying it cannot find how to cancel an incorrect medical order. A researcher concludes, “The nurses must be unfamiliar with computers.” Which response best follows task-based usability testing?

A. Send the nurses to computer training and end the test.

B. Tell them which button to press and record a pass after they succeed.

C. Record where they get stuck, ask how they understood the situation, propose a design improvement hypothesis, and retest.

D. Keep the interface because the program tests passed.

Usability depends on whether target users can complete work effectively, efficiently, and with reasonable confidence in a specific context. Improve it using observed behavior, rather than relying only on a developer’s intuition.

exercise.environment: A working local third slice, one voluntary peer, synthetic task cards and a blank record.
steps: Explain purpose and recording, obtain agreement, then give tasks without revealing button actions.
Observe omission, correction and change; record assistance, completion and actual behavior.
Separate observations from interpretations and propose one improvement hypothesis; after changing it, arrange another trial with the same goal.
exercise.expected: An anonymous task-observation record and testable design hypothesis; mark unexecuted if no person has tried it.
exercise.check: Invent no participants or results. Do not generalize one peer observation to all users.
exercise.cleanup: Stop the test service, retain anonymous records as explained and delete unnecessary synthetic downloads.

zh.prompt: 護士找不到取消錯誤醫囑的方式，研究員認為她們不熟悉電腦。哪種處理符合任務導向易用性測試？
options: 先請護士參加電腦教育訓練，再結束測試
告訴護士按哪個按鈕，只要成功就記錄通過
記錄卡住的操作、詢問當時理解，再提出介面改善假設並重新測試
因為程式測試通過，所以不用修改介面
rationales: 能力原因尚未查證；先記錄實際困難。
提供提示後應記為協助完成，並保留提示內容。
C 正確：將觀察與原因推論分開，再以測試驗證設計假設。
功能運作與使用者能否完成任務需分別驗證。

en.prompt: Nurses cannot find how to cancel an incorrect order. A researcher attributes this to poor computer skills. What should the team do?
options: Send the nurses to training and end the test.
Identify the button and count their success as a pass.
Record the difficulty, ask about their understanding, hypothesize an interface improvement, and retest.
Keep the interface because program tests passed.
rationales: The proposed cause is unverified; record the actual difficulty first.
Record assisted completion and preserve the prompt.
C is correct: separate observation from inference and test the design hypothesis.
Working functions and users completing tasks require separate evidence.
